scLimbsAbsentFromACT: TRIGGER / APPLICABILITY GATE — author-controlled additional content that appears AND disappears 'in coordination with keyboard focus or pointer hover' (Understanding Intent). The whole applicability predicate is untested: 0 ACT rules, 0 test cases.

EXCLUSION: User-Agent-controlled content — 'This criterion does not attempt to solve such issues when the appearance of the additional content is completely controlled by the user agent... the common behavior of browsers to display the title attribute in HTML as a small tooltip' (Additional Notes). No case distinguishes a native title tooltip (out of scope / passes) from an author-built tooltip.

EXCLUSION: Modal dialogs out of scope — 'Modal dialogs are out of scope for this criterion because they must take keyboard focus and thus should not appear on hover or focus' (Additional Notes). No applicability/N-A case for modals.

DISMISSIBLE condition (Method 1: positioning) — 'Position the additional content so that it does not obscure any other content including the trigger, with the exception of white space and purely decorative content' (Dismissible). No case tests obscuring vs. non-obscuring placement.

DISMISSIBLE condition (Method 2: dismiss mechanism) — 'Provide a mechanism to easily dismiss the additional content, such as by pressing Escape' (Dismissible). No case tests presence/absence of an Esc/keyboard dismissal without moving hover/focus.

DISMISSIBLE exception: input error messages — 'The success criterion allows for input error messages to persist as there are cases that require attention, explicit confirmation or remedial action' (Dismissible). This exception is entirely untested.

HOVERABLE condition — 'additional content which may appear on hover of a target may also be hovered itself' / pointer can be moved onto the new content without it disappearing (Hoverable; F95). The single normative failure technique F95 has NO corresponding ACT rule or test case in the corpus.

PERSISTENT condition — content 'should remain visible until: the user removes hover or focus...; the user dismisses the additional content...; or the information conveyed... becomes invalid' (Persistent). None of the three persistence-end conditions, nor the auto-dismiss-on-timeout failure (SCR39 test 'does not automatically close after a time'), is tested.

FOCUS path of the trigger — 'Content which can be triggered via pointer hover should also be able to be triggered by keyboard focus' and SCR39's separate focus-appears checklist (#1 persistent, #2 dismissible without moving focus). The keyboard-focus-triggered variant is wholly absent.

EN 301 549 C.9.1.4.13 — a pure WCAG-2.2 pass-through ('Check that the web page does not fail WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.13... according to clause 9.6'); it adds no new limbs but is itself unexercised since no case exists.
varietyGaps: TOTAL ABSENCE: SC 1.4.13 has 0 in-scope ACT rules and 0 local test cases (testCaseCountsByExpected = {}). Every limb of the SC is uncovered — there is no passed/failed/inapplicable example to anchor any check. This is the single largest gap.

No UI-PATTERN coverage at all. The Understanding Intent enumerates the canonical triggers — 'custom tooltips, sub-menus and other non-modal popups which display on hover and focus' — plus Examples 1-2 (LVTF dismissible tooltip, hoverable tooltip below a button) and SCR39's link content-preview popup and F95's hover popup / data-point chart popup. NONE of these patterns (tooltip, submenu/flyout menu, link preview, charted data-point popup) exists as a test fixture.

No CONTENT-DOMAIN variety: the SC's worked examples involve a button+tooltip, a link+preview popup, and a chart with hoverable data points (F95). The corpus has zero of these; there are no plain-text, form, table, media, SVG, or canvas fixtures for 1.4.13.

No OUTCOME variety: cannot exercise pass vs. fail vs. not-applicable. Missing both the failing cases the F* failure technique enables (F95: hover content not hoverable; SCR39 implies fails for auto-timeout dismissal and for no-Esc dismissal) and the sufficient/passing case (SCR39 working example).

No APPLICABILITY-boundary fixtures: the two explicit out-of-scope carve-outs (native UA title tooltip; modal dialog) and the in-scope vs out-of-scope author distinction have no negative/N-A fixtures, so the gating logic is entirely unmodeled.

No INPUT-MODALITY split: hover-triggered vs. keyboard-focus-triggered content require different SCR39 checklists (hover = hoverable+persistent+dismissible; focus = persistent+dismissible). The corpus tests neither modality.

No LOW-VISION / MAGNIFICATION scenario, which is the SC's core motivation (Dismissible/Hoverable/Benefits all cite magnified viewport and large-pointer obscuring) — no fixture exercises content that obscures the trigger or content too large to read without panning.

aspects.title: F95 — author hover content is not itself hoverable (pop-up vanishes on the cursor path from trigger to content)
aspects.description: The single normative failure technique for 1.4.13 (F95) describes author-built additional content that appears on pointer hover but DISAPPEARS the moment the user moves the pointer off the trigger toward the content to read it — because visibility is bound only to mouseover/mouseout on the trigger, there is a physical gap between trigger and pop-up, or there is no shared hover region. Judging this is a SPATIAL + BEHAVIORAL call: a reviewer mentally traces the cursor path and asks whether the pop-up is reachable without the mouseout firing. A static checker sees a span[role=tooltip] that toggles display:none on mouseout and cannot tell whether the content overlaps/adjoins the trigger or is separated by a dead-zone; the Understanding states the passing arrangement 'generally implies that the additional content overlaps or is positioned adjacent to the target.' This is the geometric/event-handler reasoning a human does by simulating pointer travel under magnification.
aspects.whyUncovered: testCaseCountsByExpected = {} — 0 ACT rules and 0 test cases for 1.4.13, so the only normative failure technique (F95) has no failing fixture and no passing counter-fixture. Nothing in the corpus exercises pointer travel from trigger to pop-up.

references.quote: A pop-up opens on pointer hover. Due to the chosen screen magnification, the content is only partially visible. However, as soon as the pointer is moved away from the trigger towards the pop-up content so it can be read, the pop-up automatically closes.
The pointer can be moved over the new content without the additional content disappearing.

A technique to view the content fully in both situations is to move the mouse pointer directly from the trigger onto the new content.  This capability also offers significant advantages for users who utilize screen reader feedback on mouse interactions.  This condition generally implies that the additional content overlaps or is positioned adjacent to the target.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained HTML pages with custom (non-title=) hover content where the hoverable condition is the variable. Bind visibility to mouseover/mouseout on the trigger only, and vary the trigger-to-popup geometry (gap vs. adjacency/overlap) and whether the popup carries its own mouseenter handler. The verdict hinges on whether a continuous pointer path keeps the content visible — a human judges this from layout + handlers; capture screenshots in hover state to confirm geometry. Include passing counter-fixtures (adjacent/overlapping popup that survives travel, or popup with its own hover handler) so PASS vs FAIL can both be anchored.
suggestedScenarios: A button with a tooltip span positioned 30px BELOW the trigger separated by a transparent gap; visibility bound to the button's mouseout — moving the cursor down to read the tooltip crosses the gap, fires mouseout, the tooltip vanishes (FAIL).

A glossary term whose definition pop-up appears on the term's mouseenter and is removed on its mouseleave, with NO mouseenter handler on the pop-up itself, so it cannot retain visibility once hovered (FAIL).
A CSS-only :hover tooltip where the tooltip element is neither a descendant of nor adjacent to the trigger, so the :hover state ends the instant the pointer leaves the trigger box (FAIL).

An SVG/HTML chart with closely-spaced data points; hovering one shows an offset details pop-up, but the path to it crosses a neighboring data point that replaces it with a different pop-up — the exact F95 chart example (FAIL).
A nav item revealing a flyout submenu offset to the right with a diagonal dead-zone; moving toward the submenu briefly leaves both hot-zones and collapses the menu before the cursor arrives (FAIL).

PASSING counter-fixture: a button whose tooltip is rendered directly adjacent/overlapping and shares a hover region (popup has its own mouseenter), so the pointer travels onto it without the content disappearing (PASS).

aspects.title: Applicability gate — author-controlled tooltip vs. user-agent title= tooltip (and modal-dialog carve-out)
aspects.description: The SC explicitly does NOT apply when the additional content's appearance is 'completely controlled by the user agent' — canonically the browser rendering of the title attribute — and modal dialogs are also out of scope. F95 bakes the UA carve-out into its test (condition #2: 'controlled by the user agent, not the author'). The judgment-heavy case is attributing WHO controls the appearance: distinguishing (a) a plain title= tooltip (out of scope, passes by exclusion) from (b) an AUTHOR-built div styled/scripted to LOOK native (in scope, must meet all three conditions) and (c) the inverse where the author suppresses the native tooltip (title='') and reimplements it in JS. A static tool sees both a title= and a div and cannot reason that the visible bubble is the author's div, not the UA's tooltip — yet getting this attribution wrong flips PASS↔FAIL for the entire criterion. The modal-dialog exclusion likewise needs an N/A judgment (a dialog takes focus, so it is not hover/focus-transient content).
aspects.whyUncovered: The exclusion carve-outs are listed as corpus gaps (no case distinguishes a native title tooltip from an author-built tooltip; no N/A case for modals). With 0 fixtures there is no example anchoring the in-scope/out-of-scope boundary, so the whole gating predicate is unmodeled.

references.quote: This criterion does not attempt to solve such issues when the appearance of the additional content is completely controlled by the user agent. A prominent example is the common behavior of browsers to display the title attribute in HTML as a small tooltip.
Modal dialogs are out of scope for this criterion because they must take keyboard focus  and thus should not appear on hover or focus.
The appearance of the additional content is controlled by the user agent, not the author.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build paired self-contained pages that are visually similar but differ in WHO controls the popup. Use real title= attributes (UA-controlled, must be judged inapplicable/PASS), author-scripted bubbles that mimic native tooltips (in scope, can FAIL), and CSS ::after / JS reimplementations of the title. Add a modal-dialog-on-focus page for the N/A carve-out. The reviewer's task is attribution — the page must contain enough evidence (presence of script handlers, custom DOM, styling) to support the judgment but not make it trivially automatable; verify with a hover screenshot that the visible bubble matches the intended owner.
suggestedScenarios: A button with ONLY title='Save your work' and no scripted pop-up — UA-controlled, out of scope, must be judged INAPPLICABLE/PASS even though it is non-hoverable.

A button with both title='Save' AND a JS-built styled bubble mimicking a native tooltip on mouseover; the author bubble is non-hoverable — in scope and FAILS, yet visually near-identical to the title= case.
An icon where the author sets title='' (suppressing the default) and reimplements an identical-looking gray bubble via CSS ::after content — author-controlled, must meet all three conditions.
An abbr title='...' (pure native, PASS by exclusion) placed next to a visually identical abbr wrapped in a scripted tooltip (in scope) — only the second is governed by the SC.
A help control whose pop-up text differs between the browser's native title rendering and an author div showing different content — the reviewer must separate which content the SC governs.
A modal dialog that opens on focus/click and takes keyboard focus — out of scope per the modal carve-out, must be judged NOT-APPLICABLE to 1.4.13.

aspects.title: Dismissible Method 2 — no/broken keyboard dismiss (cannot clear content without moving hover or focus)
aspects.description: SCR39 requires hover content 'can be closed without moving the pointer away from the trigger' and focus content 'closed without moving the focus away from the trigger' — by Esc, another documented shortcut, or activating the trigger. The judgment-heavy failures: (a) NO dismiss mechanism at all, so the user must physically move the pointer/focus to clear it, defeating the low-vision pan workaround; (b) an Esc handler scoped wrong (e.g., bound to the trigger which has lost focus, so Esc is inert while the bubble shows); (c) a 'close' that only works by moving focus INTO the pop-up, which can re-obscure. A static tool can detect that a keydown listener exists but cannot judge whether pressing Esc actually clears THIS content while hover/focus is retained on the trigger — that requires interpreting handler scope against the user's physical situation. The Understanding's whole motivation is the magnified user who cannot afford to move the pointer to dismiss obscuring text.
aspects.whyUncovered: The Dismissible-mechanism limb is listed as absent — no case tests presence/absence of an Esc/keyboard dismissal without moving hover/focus. With no fixtures there is no failing 'no-Esc' or 'wrongly-scoped-Esc' example.

references.quote: The content can be closed without moving the pointer way from the trigger. Either by pressing <kbd>Esc</kbd>, by pressing another documented keyboard shortcut, or by activating the trigger.
Provide a mechanism to easily dismiss the additional content, such as by pressing Escape.

low vision users who can only navigate via the keyboard do not want the small area of their magnified viewport cluttered with hover text. They need a keyboard method of dismissing something that is obscuring the current focal area.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages where content obscures other content (so Method 1 is NOT satisfied and the dismiss mechanism is load-bearing), then vary the dismiss path. Cases with no Esc handler, an Esc handler bound to an element that has lost focus, and a close affordance reachable only by Tab-into the popup all FAIL; a correctly-scoped document-level Esc that clears the content while the trigger keeps hover/focus PASSES. The reviewer must trace handler scope vs. where focus actually is. Verify by driving keyboard (focus trigger, press Esc) and screenshotting before/after to confirm whether the content actually clears without moving focus.
suggestedScenarios: A tooltip on a focused button that obscures content below it and has NO Esc handler — focus must be moved away to clear it (FAIL Dismissible).
A tooltip with a keydown Esc handler bound to the trigger element, but the trigger has lost DOM focus to the page body, so Esc never reaches the handler and the bubble stays (FAIL).
A pop-up whose only 'close' is an X button INSIDE the pop-up reachable only by Tab-into the pop-up — dismissing requires moving focus into the content, violating the condition (FAIL).
A hover tooltip on a non-focusable span where Esc is captured only when an input is focused; with the span hovered there is no focused element, so Esc is inert (FAIL).
A submenu dismissible only by clicking elsewhere (moving the pointer off), with no keyboard/Esc path — fails for keyboard-only magnifier users (FAIL).
PASSING counter-fixture: a document-level keydown Esc handler that hides the popup while the trigger retains hover/focus, matching the SCR39 working example (PASS).

aspects.title: Dismissible Method 1 — pop-up obscures meaningful content (beyond the white-space / decorative exception)
aspects.description: When no dismiss mechanism is provided, the SC can still be met if the content is positioned 'so that it does not obscure any other content including the trigger, with the exception of white space and purely decorative content.' This is a VISUAL + SEMANTIC judgment: does the pop-up cover meaningful content/controls, or only white space or a 'background graphic which provides no information'? A checker can compute that two boxes overlap, but cannot judge whether the covered region is purely decorative versus information-bearing. It also cannot apply the Understanding's nuance that for a LARGE trigger, positioning content away to avoid overlap may itself harm discoverability, so only Method 2 is appropriate — meaning 'obscures the trigger/content' is not always disqualifying. Distinguishing acceptable overlap of decorative whitespace from unacceptable obscuring of content is squarely human and visual.
aspects.whyUncovered: The positioning/obscuring limb is listed as absent — no case tests obscuring vs. non-obscuring placement, and there is no low-vision/magnification fixture exercising content that obscures the trigger or adjacent meaningful content.

references.quote: Position the additional content so that it does not obscure any other content including the trigger, with the exception of white space and purely decorative content, such as a background graphic which provides no information.

For most triggers of relatively small size, it is desirable for both methods to be implemented.  If the trigger is large, noticing the additional content may be of concern if it appears away from the trigger.  In those cases, only the second method may be appropriate.

It does however obscure content below the button (the next red button, called ~comment-zoom-content). To meet the Dismissible requirement, a user can press the Escape key to clear the tooltip without moving the mouse

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages where NO keyboard dismiss exists (so Method 1 is the only path to compliance), then vary WHAT the popup overlaps. The verdict requires the reviewer to identify the covered region as meaningful (body text, form fields, the trigger label) vs. exempt (white margin, purely decorative background). Render in hover/focus state and screenshot so the overlap target is visually inspectable. Include the large-trigger nuance fixture to test the 'Method 2 only' reasoning. Provide both FAIL (covers information) and PASS (covers only whitespace/decoration) anchors.
suggestedScenarios: A tooltip positioned directly OVER the next paragraph of body text, with no Esc dismiss — obscures meaningful content (FAIL Dismissible).
A tooltip overlapping the trigger button's own label so the user can no longer read what they hovered, with no dismiss path (FAIL).
A pop-up that lands on a region of pure white margin / empty grid gutter — geometric overlap exists but covers only white space (PASS by the exception).
A tooltip covering only a purely-decorative background SVG flourish that conveys no information — overlap exempt by the decorative carve-out (PASS).
A tooltip covering an adjacent form field's required-asterisk and helper text — obscuring information-bearing content (FAIL).

A large hero-card trigger whose tooltip appears far below over real content — tests the 'large trigger, only Method 2 appropriate' nuance where moving content away to avoid overlap is itself problematic.

aspects.title: Persistent — auto-dismiss on timeout / closing for a disallowed reason vs. legitimate info-invalidation
aspects.description: SCR39 requires the content 'stays visible and does not automatically close after a time,' and the Understanding says it should remain until exactly one of: the user removes hover/focus, the user dismisses it, OR the conveyed information becomes invalid (e.g., a 'busy' message). The judgment-heavy failures: (a) a tooltip on a setTimeout that auto-hides after N seconds while the user is still hovering/focused (a magnifier user needs that time to change magnification and pan); (b) content that closes for the WRONG reason (scroll, slight pointer jitter within the trigger); versus the legitimate exception — (c) content that disappears because its info BECAME INVALID (a 'saving…' that becomes 'saved'), which must NOT be flagged. Telling a disallowed timeout from a legitimate information-invalidation requires understanding the MEANING of the content over time — a human reasoning, not a timer-presence check. A static checker that merely sees setTimeout cannot tell which case it is.
aspects.whyUncovered: The Persistent limb is listed as absent — none of the three persistence-end conditions, nor the auto-dismiss-on-timeout failure ('does not automatically close after a time'), is tested; there is no outcome variety to anchor the valid-info-invalidation exception.

references.quote: The additional content stays visible and does not automatically close after a time.
Once it appears, the content should remain visible until:
The information conveyed by the additional content becomes invalid, such as a 'busy' message that is no longer valid.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages where the popup's lifetime is the variable. Use setTimeout to auto-hide while hover/focus is retained (FAIL), scroll/mousemove listeners that hide it for disallowed reasons (FAIL), and a semantically-changing message whose disappearance reflects information becoming invalid (PASS exception). The reviewer must reason about WHY the content closed and whether the underlying information is still valid — that requires reading the content's meaning, not just detecting a timer. Drive the page (hover, wait, scroll) and screenshot the timeline to confirm the disappearance trigger.
suggestedScenarios: A tooltip that fades out via setTimeout after 3 seconds even while the trigger is still hovered/focused — auto-close-after-time (FAIL).
A focus-triggered help bubble that auto-dismisses on a 5s interval while the field still has focus — fails the focus checklist item #1 (FAIL).
A tooltip that vanishes the instant the user scrolls the page (scroll listener hides it) though hover is retained — closes for a disallowed reason (FAIL).
A tooltip that disappears on the next mousemove anywhere on the page (jitter-sensitive) — a magnifier user moving the pointer to pan loses it prematurely (FAIL).
A 'busy/saving…' message that disappears when it becomes 'saved' — legitimate info-invalidation, must be judged a PASS, not a persistence failure (PASS exception).
A countdown 'offer expires in 10s' pop-up whose disappearance IS the valid information becoming invalid — exception case that should PASS (PASS exception).

aspects.title: Perceive-on-focus — hover-triggered content with NO keyboard-focus path to reveal it
aspects.description: The Additional Notes require that 'content which can be triggered via pointer hover should also be able to be triggered by keyboard focus' (cross-referencing 2.1.1), because the SC's core intent is that users can PERCEIVE the additional content; if the only reveal is mouse hover, keyboard and many AT users can never perceive it. The judgment is semantic and two-part: the reviewer must (a) recognize that the hover content carries information not otherwise available (not redundant decoration) AND (b) determine the trigger is non-focusable or has no focus handler. A static tool can note that a tooltip is bound to mouseover-but-not-focus, but cannot judge whether the trigger SHOULD be focusable (is it interactive? is the content meaningful?) — recognizing 'this hidden content matters and is unreachable by keyboard' is a contextual call. This is the focus-modality half of SCR39, which carries a DIFFERENT checklist than hover (persistent + dismissible only; no hoverable requirement).
aspects.whyUncovered: The keyboard-focus-triggered variant is listed as wholly absent, and there is no input-modality split in the corpus (hover vs. focus require different SCR39 checklists). With 0 fixtures, the focus path of the trigger is entirely unmodeled.

references.quote: Content which can be triggered via pointer hover should also be able to be triggered by keyboard focus. Refer to Success Criterion 2.1.1 Keyboard.
the user may not know new content has appeared
For additional content that appears on focus check that:

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages where meaningful information (not redundant labels) is revealed ONLY on mouseover, then vary whether a keyboard-focus path exists. Non-focusable triggers (span/div, no tabindex, no focus handler) revealing real content FAIL; the same content reachable on focus PASSES. Include a redundancy decoy (hover content that merely repeats visible text) to test the 'is this content meaningful' half of the judgment. The reviewer must combine content-meaning assessment with focus-reachability. Verify by Tab-navigating the page and screenshotting focus state to confirm whether the content ever appears for keyboard users.
suggestedScenarios: An info icon (non-focusable span, no tabindex) that reveals a definition pop-up only on mouseover — keyboard users can never perceive the content (FAIL).
A chart data-point (div) whose details pop-up is bound to mouseenter only, with no focus/keyboard equivalent — meaningful data unreachable by keyboard (FAIL).
A custom tooltip on a focusable button bound to mouseover but NOT to focus/focusin — interactive trigger, content carries unique info, no keyboard reveal (FAIL).
A glossary term with a hover-only definition popup where the same definition appears nowhere else on the page — unique information lost to keyboard users (FAIL).

A DECOY hover bubble that merely repeats the trigger's already-visible visible label — content is redundant, so absence of a focus path may not harm perception (judgment: likely PASS / not a 1.4.13 perceive failure).
PASSING counter-fixture: a tooltip bound to BOTH mouseover and focusin on a focusable trigger, revealing the same meaningful content for hover and keyboard users (PASS).

pages.scenario: SaaS billing page: a "?" help button beside "Seat overage" shows a custom tooltip positioned 30px BELOW the trigger, separated by a transparent .gap spacer (pointer-events:none). Show/hide is bound only to the trigger button's mouseover/mouseout; the tooltip has no hover handler and is not a descendant of the trigger. Moving the pointer down to read the tooltip crosses the gap, fires mouseout, and the tooltip vanishes before the pointer reaches it.
pages.mechanism: Hoverable (F95) pure dead-zone: trigger-to-popup geometry is a transparent gap (top:50px on a 20px trigger with a 30px spacer), not adjacency/overlap, and the popup carries no mouseenter, so the trigger's mouseout fires on the travel path and hides the tooltip; no continuous pointer path keeps the content visible.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No engine implements 1.4.13. The markup is impeccable (real <button>, role=tooltip, aria-describedby, appears on focus, ~16:1 contrast), so a "tooltip toggles on hover" heuristic passes. Catching it requires mentally tracing the pointer from the 20px trigger down across a 30px transparent gap and reasoning that mouseout fires before the pointer arrives — a spatial + event-handler simulation no static checker performs. Verified in Puppeteer: tip visible on trigger, hidden after pointer enters the gap.

citation.quote: A pop-up opens on pointer hover. Due to the chosen screen magnification, the content is only partially visible. However, as soon as the pointer is moved away from the trigger towards the pop-up content so it can be read, the pop-up automatically closes.

pages.scenario: Community forum thread: a GitHub/Twitter-style profile "hover card" appears when hovering a username. It is rendered into a detached portal layer (#hovercard-layer, sibling of the content) positioned 12px below the username. Show is delayed 180ms (hover-intent); hide is immediate on the username's mouseleave; the card has no mouseenter of its own. Moving the pointer down to the card crosses the 12px transparent gap, fires mouseleave, and the card vanishes instantly.
pages.mechanism: Hoverable (F95) with timing asymmetry: delayed-show / immediate-hide, popup is a portal sibling (no DOM proximity to the trigger), a 12px transparent gap sits on the travel path, and there is no popup mouseenter to cancel the hide — so a continuous pointer path cannot keep the card open.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No 1.4.13 rule exists, and the portal actively misleads a DOM-proximity heuristic (the card is nowhere near the trigger in the DOM, yet that does not help). The card is statically exemplary: role=dialog, aria-label, real controls, good contrast, opens on focus. The failure requires reasoning jointly about the 180ms-show/instant-hide asymmetry, the 12px gap, and the missing card mouseenter — a behavioral+geometric pointer-travel simulation. Verified in Puppeteer: card shows after delay, hidden after pointer enters the gap.

citation.quote: When the added content is large, magnified views may mean that the user needs to scroll or pan to completely view it, which is impossible unless the user is able to move their pointer off the trigger without the additional content disappearing.

pages.scenario: Fintech dashboard: an SVG line chart of daily NAV where each <circle> data point shows a detail pop-up on mouseenter, offset above-and-right of the point. Points are closely spaced (~26px) and share one reusable pop-up. To read the offset pop-up for a point under magnification, the pointer must travel toward it — crossing the next data point, whose mouseenter replaces the wanted pop-up with the neighbour's (the exact F95 chart example).
pages.mechanism: Hoverable (F95) chart variant: the pop-up is offset (+14,-46) from its point with pointer-events:none and there is no shared hover region; because adjacent points are ~26px apart, the cursor path to one pop-up crosses a neighbour whose mouseenter re-renders the shared pop-up, destroying the one the user wanted.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No 1.4.13 rule, and the page passes the checks a scanner can do (svg role=img + aria-label, a real <table> data fallback for 1.1.1, focusable points with handlers for 2.1.1). The failure is purely a function of pixel geometry — point spacing vs. pop-up offset vs. which point the travel vector intersects. Verified in Puppeteer: pop-up read "Jun 11 $1.041 +1.0%" then changed to "Jun 12 $1.037 -0.4%" when crossing the neighbour.

citation.quote: Hovering over a chart with data points, pop-ups open to show details of the respective data point, somewhat offset from the data point itself. When moving the pointer towards the pop-up so it can be fully read with magnification, the pointer travels over other data points that cause the appearance of other pop-ups that replace the particular pop-up the user wanted to see.

pages.scenario: E-commerce category sidebar: hovering a top-level category ("Camp & Hike") reveals a CSS-only flyout submenu offset to the right (left:230px against a 210px row, leaving a ~20px transparent corridor). The flyout is a DOM child of the category but not geometrically contiguous; reaching lower submenu items requires a diagonal down-and-right path that exits both hot-zones, ending the :hover state and collapsing the flyout before the cursor arrives.
pages.mechanism: Hoverable (F95) diagonal dead-zone: popup is a DOM descendant (li.cat:hover > .flyout) but positioned with a horizontal gap and a taller box, so the natural diagonal travel vector passes through empty space belonging to neither li.cat nor .flyout; :hover on li.cat goes false and the CSS reveal rule stops matching mid-travel. No JS hover-intent bridge spans the corner.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No 1.4.13 rule, and the most plausible static heuristic is fooled: the flyout IS a DOM child of the trigger, so "popup nested in trigger? probably hoverable" passes — yet DOM nesting does not imply geometric contiguity here. Markup is a clean nested ul/role=group with good contrast and :focus-within keyboard reveal. Judging it requires tracing a realistic diagonal pointer path against the two bounding boxes and the 20px gap. Verified in Puppeteer: flyout visible on hover, hidden when the pointer sits in the diagonal corridor.

citation.quote: A technique to view the content fully in both situations is to move the mouse pointer directly from the trigger onto the new content.  This capability also offers significant advantages for users who utilize screen reader feedback on mouse interactions.  This condition generally implies that the additional content overlaps or is positioned adjacent to the target.

pages.scenario: Pharmacy prescription page: a glossary term <dfn> ("contraindication") shows a definition pop-up that DIRECTLY overlaps/adjoins the term (top:-2px, no gap) — visually the passing arrangement the Understanding describes. But the pop-up carries pointer-events:none and reveal is keyed only to the term's :hover, so moving the pointer onto the pop-up means the cursor is no longer counted as over the term, :hover collapses, and the content vanishes. Adjacency is present but the content is not actually hoverable.
pages.mechanism: Hoverable (F95) "adjacency present but un-hoverable": geometry satisfies overlap/adjacency, yet pointer-events:none makes the popup transparent to the cursor; the pointer entering the popup region is not counted as hovering the trigger, so dfn.term:hover .def stops matching and the popup hides. There is no continuous pointer path despite perfect visual adjacency.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No 1.4.13 rule, and this case specifically defeats the smarter heuristics: a geometry/overlap check passes (the overlap is real) and a markup review passes (<dfn>, role=tooltip, aria-describedby, tabindex, focus parity, ~15:1 contrast). The single breaking line, pointer-events:none, is a common harmless tooltip style; no linter knows it makes a hover-revealed popup un-hoverable. Catching it requires reasoning about CSS hit-testing — that the cursor over the popup is not hovering the trigger. citation.quote: The intent of this condition is to ensure that additional content which may appear on hover of a target may also be hovered itself.  Content which appears on hover can be difficult or impossible to perceive if a user is required to keep their mouse pointer over the trigger.
